column3: The Hebrew begins the reply “Because I was afraid.”
The Hebrew does not separately add “here” and calls the relatives “our brothers.”
The Hebrew has one “tent of the two maidservants,” rather than “tents.”
The Hebrew says Laban felt through “the whole tent,” rather than “everything in the tent.”
The Hebrew preserves the expressions “in the eyes of my lord” and “the way of women is upon me.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew asks what he found “of all the things of your house.”
The Hebrew specifically names ewes and female goats.
The Hebrew retains the image “from my hand you demanded it.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew first says “these twenty years in your house,” then states his service for the daughters and flock.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew puts “I and you” in that order.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the relatives his “brothers.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “he called its name Galeed,” rather than making “the place” the explicit subject.
The Hebrew describes being “hidden from one another,” rather than simply absent.
The Hebrew says “wives besides my daughters” and “see,” rather than “remember.”
The Hebrew repeats “behold” before both the mound and the pillar.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew verb “judge” is plural, matching the two divine designations in the request.
The Hebrew repeats “bread” for the invitation and the eating, rather than the more general “meal.”
The Hebrew says “his sons,” rather than “his grandchildren,” and repeats Laban’s name before his departure.
